description: I'm building Flame to Lung a dashboard that follows NASA’s microgravity fire experiments from the first overheated wire to the smoke a crew member breathes, with a 3D lung model and an AI assistant that only quotes NASA data.
summary:
Flame to Lung is an interactive dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight, following a spacecraft fire from the first overheated wire to the smoke a crew member breathes.

It organizes six NASA investigations (SAME, FLEX, BASS, BASS-II, Saffire and SPICE) into ranked findings, side-by-side comparisons, and a materials map that shows where flammability and smoke data are missing. Two predictive models let users explore scenarios: a machine-learning flame simulator, trained on 257 FLEX droplet burns, predicts whether a flame survives in a given atmosphere, how much fuel it leaves behind, and what change would make it safer; a physics-based lung model predicts where smoke particles deposit in the lungs under Earth, lunar and orbital gravity. An AI assistant answers questions using only these data and models, labelling every number as measured, modelled or a recommendation.
details:
Flame to Lung is a web dashboard with six sections:

  1. Investigations: nine findings ranked for fire safety with a visible scoring method, plus summary cards and a side-by-side comparison of each NASA experiment’s objective, fuels, test conditions, measurements and hardware.
  2. Materials: an evidence map of which materials were tested for burning and which for smoke. Only cotton and silicone have both, and every gap is marked.
  3. Flame science: measured comparisons of fuels, diluent gases (nitrogen, CO₂, helium), soot tendency, and the fuel left unburned when a visible flame goes out, an indicator of cool-flame and re-ignition risk.
  4. Flame simulator: a machine-learning model trained on 257 FLEX droplet burns. The user sets fuel, oxygen, diluents, pressure and droplet size; it predicts the chance the flame goes out early, the burning rate and the fuel left behind, then recommends the changes that would make the fire safer.
  5. Lung model: a physics model that combines NASA’s measured smoke particle sizes with the ICRP 66 lung deposition model, a smoke-aging model fitted to SAME data, and a gravity correction, to estimate where smoke deposits in the lungs on Earth, the Moon and in orbit.
  6. Assistant: a conversational AI that answers only by calling tools over the data and models, labelling every number as Measured, Modeled or Recommendation.

Benefits and intended impact

Researchers and students can explore decades of experiments in minutes instead of reading separate datasets. Engineers can test “what if” scenarios such as a 30% oxygen Moon-base atmosphere. The project also surfaces a result that is easy to miss: lowering oxygen makes a flame more likely to go out but leaves more unburned fuel behind, so a fire that looks extinguished may not be safe. The gap map points to experiments worth flying next.

Tools used

Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Flask), JavaScript, Three.js for the 3D flame and lung, Plotly for charts, and a hosted open-weight language model through an OpenAI-compatible API. Data comes from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics system (PSI-25, 26, 69, 98–102, 107). Development was done in GitHub Codespaces, with AI tools assisting the coding and writing.

How it is creative

Our tool follows the fire to the crew’s lungs, linking combustion data to human exposure. The interface is built around a live 3D scene: a spherical microgravity flame that responds to the simulator, and a particle lung that lights up where smoke deposits.

Factors considered

Every result is traceable to a NASA file or a named model, models report their validation scores, and predictions outside the tested range are flagged. The limits are stated on the site: the flame model covers fuel droplets, not solid materials; cool-flame temperatures are not in the data; deposition is not toxicity; toxic gases are not modelled; and PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data yet.
